title: Units conversions and data provenance

prerequisite.answer: 3 minutes, since 60 seconds make one minute.

vocabulary: The origin and processing history of data
Expressing a quantity in another unit
A value calculated from recorded data

blocks.text: Two fictional activity logs use different duration units. Log A records 180 seconds and Log B records 4 minutes. Keep the raw values, units and source labels; derive a shared unit so another learner can reproduce the comparison.

blocks.title: Python 3 code
Follow the evidence

blocks.text: The script prints [3.0, 4]. The slash operator returns a floating-point result. The original dictionaries are unchanged. Assume nonnegative numeric raw values have already been validated. An unsupported unit produces None here and must be reported for review rather than included in arithmetic.

blocks.label: Convert 90 seconds and 0 seconds. Which is longer: 90 seconds or 2 minutes?

blocks.text: Comparing raw 180 to raw 4 ignores their units. Dividing 4 by 60 without checking its unit is also wrong: it was already minutes. Branch on the documented unit and keep a conversion note.
Correct conversion does not establish that the sources measured the same activity, used the same start and stop rules, or are accurate. Provenance helps someone investigate those differences.

workbook.title: Retain the source
workbook.prompt: Name four pieces of information to keep for Log A and its conversion.
workbook.answer: Source A, raw 180, unit seconds and derived 3.0 minutes; also record divide by 60.

workbook.title: Convert precisely
workbook.prompt: Convert 150 seconds and 30 seconds to minutes without rounding to whole numbers.

workbook.title: Repair a comparison
workbook.prompt: A report claims 120 seconds exceeds 3 minutes because 120 > 3. Correct it.
workbook.answer: 120 seconds is 2 minutes, so 3 minutes is longer.

workbook.title: Normalize independently
workbook.prompt: Create records for 240 seconds, 1.5 minutes and 60 seconds. Derive minutes while keeping raw data. State the values and their total.
workbook.answer: 4.0, 1.5 and 1.0 minutes; total 6.5 minutes. Retain original units and values.

workbook.title: Handle an unknown unit
workbook.prompt: A record contains value 8 and unit ticks with no conversion rule. Should you assume seconds?
workbook.answer: No. Mark it unresolved and ask for the unit definition. Do not include it as a known duration.

teacher.background: Teach Week 15 as a two-session investigation using fictional data. Two fictional activity logs use different duration units. Log A records 180 seconds and Log B records 4 minutes. Keep the raw values, units and source labels; derive a shared unit so another learner can reproduce the comparison. Assess the three stated outcomes through the independent task, not by copying the worked result.
materials: Python 3 editor with a fresh local practice file
Paper trace table and the student workbook
Fictional input records from this lesson; no real student identifiers

misconceptions: A successful run proves the conclusion
Correct conversion does not establish that the sources measured the same activity, used the same start and stop rules, or are accurate. Provenance helps someone investigate those differences.
Require the new W4 case, explicit predictions and an explanation. Fresh retry: 90 seconds, 2 minutes and 30 seconds become 1.5, 2, 0.5; total 4 minutes. Keep the three source records.
Comparing raw 180 to raw 4 ignores their units. Dividing 4 by 60 without checking its unit is also wrong: it was already minutes. Branch on the documented unit and keep a conversion note.
teacher.assessment: Independent W4 evidence: 4.0, 1.5 and 1.0 minutes; total 6.5 minutes. Retain original units and values. Record whether the learner needed no help, a hint or explanation. Fresh retry: 90 seconds, 2 minutes and 30 seconds become 1.5, 2, 0.5; total 4 minutes. Keep the three source records.
